title: European data center boom risks higher energy bills, Moody's warns
source_used: The Register (ET Datacenters read as well)
key_facts: Moody's, the credit rating agency, forecasts that data centers will take a growing share of Europe's electricity by 2035, potentially pushing up consumer prices and prompting government price caps or restrictions.
Data centers took 'a low single-digit share' of electricity in most large European markets in 2025, typically about 2.5 percent.
Moody's estimates data centers will account for at least 5.7 percent of electricity demand in France and the UK by 2035, up to 17 percent in the Netherlands and 30 percent in Ireland.
Ireland is an outlier: data centers already used 23 percent of its electricity in 2025, up from 5 percent in 2015.
The EU aims to more than triple its data center capacity within five to seven years and to spread projects beyond Germany, Ireland, France and the Netherlands to the Nordics and southern Europe.

The cost of expanding grids plus supply and demand imbalances is set to push energy prices higher, Moody's forecasts; some governments are weighing tax cuts and subsidies for users, and more grid operators demand financial guarantees to screen out speculative projects.
Intervention could become more intrusive, for example price caps, extra taxes or levies; Ireland now requires large new data centers to bring matching power generation or storage.
quote_evidence: Datacenters are forecast to consume a growing share of Europe's electricity by 2035, potentially pushing up consumer prices and prompting governments to impose price caps or restrictions on bit barns, according to Moody's.

The report estimates datacenters will account for at least 5.7 percent of electricity demand in France and the UK by 2035, but could be as high as 17 percent for the Netherlands and 30 percent for Ireland.
Moody's expects more European governments to intervene if data center expansion continues on its current trajectory.
why_it_matters_hint: A rating agency expects data center power demand to push up European electricity bills and prompt government intervention.
notes: Pool source ET Datacenters was readable (HTTP 200) but The Register reported the Moody's study first (13 Oct, 10:30 UTC) and with more detail, so The Register is credited. These are forecasts to 2035, not measured results.
